theory.overview: Virtual Machines (VMs) bridge the gap between high-level code and physical hardware. Rather than compiling directly to machine code, many modern languages (Java, Python, JavaScript, C#) compile to an intermediate bytecode—a portable, low-level instruction set. The VM interprets or compiles this bytecode at runtime, providing portability, security, and sophisticated runtime services like garbage collection and JIT optimization. Understanding VMs reveals how languages achieve 'write once, run anywhere' and enables optimization insights.

sections.title: Why Virtual Machines?
sections.content: VMs solve critical problems in language implementation. Portability: bytecode runs on any platform with a VM implementation. Safety: the VM can enforce memory bounds, type safety, and access controls before executing code. Runtime Services: VMs provide garbage collection, exception handling, and reflection uniformly. Dynamic Features: late binding, dynamic loading, and runtime code generation become possible. The trade-off is some performance overhead, though JIT compilation and advanced optimization narrow this gap significantly.

sections.title: Bytecode Fundamentals
sections.content: Bytecode is a compact, numeric instruction set designed for efficient interpretation. Unlike text-based source code, bytecode uses single-byte opcodes (hence 'bytecode') with optional operands. Instructions typically manipulate a stack (stack-based VMs like JVM) or registers (register-based VMs like Lua). Common instructions include PUSH, POP, ADD, SUB, LOAD, STORE, JUMP, CALL, and RETURN. Each instruction is simple—complex operations are built by composing these primitives.
keyPoints: Data Movement: LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP, CONST
Arithmetic: ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, MOD, NEG
Comparison: EQ, NE, LT, GT, LE, GE
Control Flow: JUMP, JUMP_IF_TRUE, JUMP_IF_FALSE, CALL, RETURN
Object/Array: NEW, GET_FIELD, SET_FIELD, GET_INDEX, SET_INDEX

sections.title: Stack-Based vs Register-Based
sections.content: Stack-based VMs (JVM, CPython, .NET CLR) use an operand stack for all operations. Instructions implicitly operate on stack top: PUSH 5, PUSH 3, ADD leaves 8 on stack. This design is simple, compact, and easy to generate code for. Register-based VMs (Lua, Dalvik) use virtual registers like hardware CPUs. ADD R1, R2, R3 adds R2+R3→R1. Register VMs typically require fewer instructions (less dispatch overhead) but larger instruction encodings. Both approaches can achieve excellent performance with JIT compilation.

sections.title: The Execution Loop
sections.content: At the heart of every interpreter VM is the execution loop: fetch the next instruction, decode its opcode, dispatch to handler code, execute, repeat. This is often called the 'interpreter loop' or 'dispatch loop'. Efficient VMs use techniques like direct threading (where each opcode is a pointer to handler code), computed GOTO (GCC extension), or switch-based dispatch. The loop continues until a HALT instruction or exception occurs.

sections.title: Constant Pool and Metadata
sections.content: Bytecode files contain more than just instructions. The constant pool stores literals (strings, numbers) referenced by index—compact and enables string interning. Metadata includes class definitions, method signatures, field descriptors, and debugging information. This enables reflection (inspecting types at runtime), serialization, and dynamic loading. The JVM's .class format and Python's .pyc files both use this structure.
keyPoints: Constant Pool: Stores shared constants and references
Method Area: Bytecode for methods and static data
Stack Frames: Per-method call: locals, operand stack, PC

keyConcepts.name: Opcode
keyConcepts.description: The instruction identifier, usually a single byte. The VM dispatch table uses this to find handler code.

keyConcepts.name: Program Counter (PC)
keyConcepts.description: Index into the current bytecode instruction. Updated by sequential execution or jump instructions.

keyConcepts.name: Operand Stack
keyConcepts.description: LIFO stack used for temporary values in stack-based VMs. Instructions implicitly pop operands and push results.

keyConcepts.name: Local Variables / Registers
keyConcepts.description: Storage for method parameters and local variables. Faster than heap access, lifetime bound to call frame.

complexity.memory: $O(d * s)$ where $d$ = call depth, $s$ = max stack size

steps.title: Load Bytecode
steps.description: Read compiled bytecode from file or memory into instruction array. Initialize constant pool.

steps.title: Initialize Execution Frame
steps.description: Create stack frame with empty operand stack, local variable array, and program counter at 0.

steps.title: Fetch Instruction
steps.description: Read opcode at current PC position. Increment PC to point to next instruction or operands.

steps.title: Decode and Execute
steps.description: Dispatch to handler based on opcode. PUSH: read operand, push to stack. ADD: pop two values, add, push result.

steps.title: Handle Control Flow
steps.description: For JUMP instructions: modify PC directly. For CALL: push new frame, set PC to method start.

steps.title: Loop Until Completion
steps.description: Repeat fetch-decode-execute cycle. Handle HALT or RETURN to exit, possibly with return value.

practiceProblems.title: Stack Evaluation
practiceProblems.description: Trace the stack after: PUSH 5, PUSH 3, ADD, PUSH 2, MUL
practiceProblems.explanation: 5 and 3 pushed, ADD pops both pushes 8. 2 pushed, MUL pops 8 and 2, pushes 16.

practiceProblems.title: Bytecode for Expression
practiceProblems.explanation: Stack-based evaluation: push 10, push 4, push 2. MUL: 4*2=8. SUB: 10-8=2.
hints: Push operands in order they appear

practiceProblems.title: Conditional Jump
practiceProblems.description: What does this do? PUSH 5, PUSH 3, LT, JUMP_IF_FALSE 10, PUSH 1, JUMP 11, (10) PUSH 0, (11) HALT
practiceProblems.answer: Pushes 1 if 5<3 (false), else pushes 0. Result: 0 on stack (since 5<3 is false)
practiceProblems.explanation: LT compares 5<3=false(0). JUMP_IF_FALSE sees 0, so jumps to 10, pushing 0.

practiceProblems.title: Function Call Frame
practiceProblems.description: What happens when a CALL instruction executes in a stack-based VM?
practiceProblems.answer: New stack frame created with: PC set to method start, fresh locals initialized, empty operand stack
practiceProblems.explanation: CALL pushes a frame with method context. RETURN pops frame and pushes return value to caller's stack.
hints: Frame = context for one method invocation

practiceProblems.title: Local Variables
practiceProblems.description: Trace: STORE_LOCAL 0 (from stack), LOAD_LOCAL 0, PUSH 5, ADD
practiceProblems.answer: If stack initially had 10: 10→local[0], load 10, push 5, ADD→15 on stack
practiceProblems.explanation: STORE_LOCAL pops stack to local variable. LOAD_LOCAL pushes local to stack. Enables variable reuse.

practiceProblems.title: Instruction Count Comparison
practiceProblems.description: For `a = b + c`, compare stack vs register VM instruction count.
practiceProblems.answer: Stack: 4-5 instructions (LOAD b, LOAD c, ADD, STORE a). Register: 1-2 (ADD a, b, c or LOAD b, ADD c, STORE a)
practiceProblems.explanation: Register VMs specify operands in instruction, reducing instruction count. Stack needs separate loads.

practiceProblems.title: Constant Pool Access
practiceProblems.description: Why do VMs use constant pool indexes instead of inline constants?
practiceProblems.answer: Saves space (large constants don't repeat), enables constant folding, supports string interning
practiceProblems.explanation: String 'hello' used 10 times = 1 pool entry + 10 small index references, not 10 full strings.

practiceProblems.title: VM vs Native Performance
practiceProblems.description: Why is interpreted bytecode slower than native machine code?
practiceProblems.answer: Dispatch overhead, stack manipulation, no hardware register optimization, indirect jumps
practiceProblems.explanation: Each instruction: fetch, decode, dispatch (software). Native: direct hardware execution. JIT helps close gap.

practiceProblems.title: Bytecode Verification
practiceProblems.description: How does the JVM bytecode verifier ensure safety before execution?
practiceProblems.answer: Static analysis checks: type safety on stack, local variable initialization, valid jumps, proper method signatures
practiceProblems.explanation: Verifier simulates execution without running, tracking stack/locals types at each instruction. Catches stack underflow, type mismatches.

practiceProblems.title: Tail Call Optimization
practiceProblems.description: How can VMs optimize tail-recursive calls to prevent stack growth?
practiceProblems.answer: Replace current frame instead of pushing new one: reuse stack frame, jump to method start
practiceProblems.explanation: When call is last action (tail position), no need to keep current frame. Jump to new method, reusing frame = constant stack space.
hints: Tail position = no work after call returns
Enables infinite recursion in fixed space

visualizer.description: Interactive VM execution visualization. Watch the program counter advance, observe stack operations, and see how bytecode translates to computation. Step through or run continuously.

snippets.title: Stack-Based VM
snippets.code:
from enum import Enum, auto
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Dict, Any

class OpCode(Enum):
    # Constants and locals
    PUSH = auto()
    POP = auto()
    LOAD_LOCAL = auto()
    STORE_LOCAL = auto()
    
    # Arithmetic
    ADD = auto()
    SUB = auto()
    MUL = auto()
    DIV = auto()
    NEG = auto()
    
    # Comparison
    EQ = auto()
    LT = auto()
    GT = auto()
    
    # Control flow
    JUMP = auto()
    JUMP_IF_FALSE = auto()
    CALL = auto()
    RETURN = auto()
    
    # I/O
    PRINT = auto()
    HALT = auto()

@dataclass
class Instruction:
    opcode: OpCode
    operand: Any = None

class VM:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack: List[Any] = []
        self.locals: Dict[int, Any] = {}
        self.pc: int = 0
        self.bytecode: List[Instruction] = []
        self.running: bool = False
        self.call_stack: List[int] = []  # Return addresses
    
    def load(self, bytecode: List[Instruction]):
        self.bytecode = bytecode
        self.pc = 0
        self.stack.clear()
        self.locals.clear()
    
    def run(self):
        self.running = True
        while self.running and self.pc < len(self.bytecode):
            instr = self.bytecode[self.pc]
            self.pc += 1
            self.execute(instr)
    
    def step(self):
        if self.pc < len(self.bytecode):
            instr = self.bytecode[self.pc]
            self.pc += 1
            self.execute(instr)
            return True
        return False
    
    def execute(self, instr: Instruction):
        op = instr.opcode
        
        if op == OpCode.PUSH:
            self.stack.append(instr.operand)
        
        elif op == OpCode.POP:
            self.stack.pop()
        
        elif op == OpCode.LOAD_LOCAL:
            self.stack.append(self.locals.get(instr.operand, 0))
        
        elif op == OpCode.STORE_LOCAL:
            self.locals[instr.operand] = self.stack.pop()
        
        elif op == OpCode.ADD:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a + b)
        
        elif op == OpCode.SUB:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a - b)
        
        elif op == OpCode.MUL:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a * b)
        
        elif op == OpCode.DIV:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(a / b if b != 0 else float('inf'))
        
        elif op == OpCode.NEG:
            self.stack.append(-self.stack.pop())
        
        elif op == OpCode.EQ:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(1 if a == b else 0)
        
        elif op == OpCode.LT:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(1 if a < b else 0)
        
        elif op == OpCode.GT:
            b = self.stack.pop()
            a = self.stack.pop()
            self.stack.append(1 if a > b else 0)
        
        elif op == OpCode.JUMP:
            self.pc = instr.operand
        
        elif op == OpCode.JUMP_IF_FALSE:
            if self.stack.pop() == 0:
                self.pc = instr.operand
        
        elif op == OpCode.CALL:
            self.call_stack.append(self.pc)
            self.pc = instr.operand
        
        elif op == OpCode.RETURN:
            if self.call_stack:
                self.pc = self.call_stack.pop()
            else:
                self.running = False
        
        elif op == OpCode.PRINT:
            print(self.stack[-1])
        
        elif op == OpCode.HALT:
            self.running = False
    
    def get_state(self):
        return {
            'pc': self.pc,
            'stack': list(self.stack),
            'locals': dict(self.locals)
        }

# Example: Compute (10 + 20) * 3
bytecode = [
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 10),
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 20),
    Instruction(OpCode.ADD),
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 3),
    Instruction(OpCode.MUL),
    Instruction(OpCode.PRINT),
    Instruction(OpCode.HALT)
]

vm = VM()
vm.load(bytecode)
print('Running: (10 + 20) * 3')
vm.run()
print(f'Final stack: {vm.stack}')

# Example: Conditional
# if 5 > 3 then print 1 else print 0
conditional_bytecode = [
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 5),
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 3),
    Instruction(OpCode.GT),
    Instruction(OpCode.JUMP_IF_FALSE, 8),  # Jump to else
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 1),
    Instruction(OpCode.PRINT),
    Instruction(OpCode.JUMP, 10),  # Skip else
    Instruction(OpCode.PUSH, 0),     # Else branch
    Instruction(OpCode.PRINT),
    Instruction(OpCode.HALT)
]

vm.load(conditional_bytecode)
print('\nRunning: if 5 > 3 then 1 else 0')
vm.run()
